games.title: Gran Trak 10
games.note: The first arcade car racing game and the first video game with a steering wheel, plus pedals and a gear stick.

games.title: Speed Race
games.note: Designed by Tomohiro Nishikado, who later made Space Invaders. Midway sold it in North America as Racer and Wheels.

games.title: Nürburgring 1
games.note: A German coin-op with a first-person view of the road, released earlier in 1976 than Atari's Night Driver.

games.title: Night Driver
games.note: One of the first games with real-time first-person graphics; the car's bonnet was a plastic overlay on the screen.

games.title: Sprint 2
games.note: A two-player top-down track racer from Atari's Kee Games label, in the style of Gran Trak 10.

games.title: Super Sprint
games.note: Three players steer tiny cars around top-down tracks, collecting wrenches to upgrade speed, traction and turbo.

games.title: Monaco GP
games.note: A top-down racer that became the most popular arcade driving game in the US.

games.title: Super Monaco GP
games.note: Formula One racing with a rear-view mirror on screen; the Mega Drive version added a full championship season.

games.title: Hang-On
games.note: Players leaned a ride-on motorbike cabinet to steer. It was the highest-grossing arcade game of 1986 in the US.

games.title: Test Drive
games.note: Exotic sports cars on a mountain road, seen from the cockpit, with a radar detector to spot police.

games.title: Hard Drivin'
games.note: One of the first 3D polygon driving games, with a loop and a jump on its stunt track.

games.title: Stunts
games.note: Also sold as 4D Sports Driving. Its built-in editor let players build tracks with loops and jumps.

games.title: Lotus Esprit Turbo Challenge
games.note: Split-screen two-player racing in a licensed Lotus Esprit; two sequels followed.

games.title: Top Gear
games.note: The screen is always split, even in single player. Barry Leitch's soundtrack made it a favourite in Brazil.

games.title: Horizon Chase
games.note: A 3D tribute to 16-bit road racers, scored by Top Gear composer Barry Leitch. Expanded as Horizon Chase Turbo in 2018.

games.title: Road Rash
games.note: Motorbike races on public roads where riders punch and club each other. Designed by Randy Breen, Dan Geisler and Walter Stein.

games.title: Skitchin'
games.note: Inline skaters grab onto passing cars to race through North American cities, fighting rivals on the way.

games.title: Virtua Racing
games.note: Developed alongside Sega's Model 1 arcade board. IGN ranked it the third most influential racing game.

games.title: Daytona USA
games.note: The first game on Sega's Model 2 board, inspired by the popularity of NASCAR. Linked cabinets let up to eight people race.

games.title: Sega Rally Championship
games.note: The first racing game where handling changed with the road surface. Produced by Tetsuya Mizuguchi.

games.title: Colin McRae Rally
games.note: Featured real cars and drivers from the 1998 World Rally Championship season.

games.title: Colin McRae: Dirt
games.note: Started the Dirt series; the McRae name was dropped after Dirt 2.

games.title: Motor Toon Grand Prix
games.note: A cartoon racer from the Sony team that went on to make Gran Turismo.

games.title: Gran Turismo 4
games.note: Online racing was planned but cut before release.

games.title: Gran Turismo 7
games.note: Released for the series' 25th anniversary; most modes need an online connection.

games.title: Forza Motorsport
games.note: Microsoft's answer to Gran Turismo; the series later spawned Forza Horizon.

games.title: Forza Horizon
games.note: Set at a fictional music festival in Colorado; Playground's first game, made with Turn 10.

games.title: Metropolis Street Racer
games.note: Recreated parts of London, Tokyo and San Francisco, and introduced Kudos points for driving with style.

games.title: Project Gotham Racing
games.note: An Xbox launch game in North America that carried Metropolis Street Racer's Kudos scoring to New York.

games.title: Burnout
games.note: Creator Alex Ward has said a car crash scene in the film Ronin inspired it.

games.title: Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit
games.note: Criterion's first Need for Speed; its Autolog system compared friends' times automatically.

links.took: Arcade car racing at the wheel; Tomohiro Nishikado was inspired by Gran Trak 10.
links.added: A scrolling road with rival cars to overtake, instead of one fixed track.
links.extra: Speed Race's vertical scrolling went on to influence Atari's Hi-way (1975).

links.took: Atari's top-down track racing with steering wheels and pedals.
links.added: Two players racing each other at once, sold under Atari's Kee Games label.
links.extra: Wikipedia groups Sprint 2 and Super Sprint as later Atari racers in the same style.

links.took: The top-down Sprint track-racing format.
links.added: Three-player cabinets, eight tracks with shortcuts, and wrenches to upgrade cars.

links.took: A first-person drive; Dave Shepperd was handed the concept of 'a German game'.
links.added: Roadside markers rushing out of the dark, and a plastic car bonnet over the screen.
links.extra: Shepperd's 'German game' was later identified as Nürburgring 1, released earlier in 1976.

links.took: Sega's Monaco GP name and Formula One-style racing.
links.added: A behind-the-car view with scaling sprites instead of the top-down track.

links.took: Pole Position popularized behind-the-car Formula One racing with a qualifying lap.
links.added: A rear-view mirror on screen and a full championship season on the Mega Drive.

links.took: Yu Suzuki's sprite-scaling road racing from Hang-On and Enduro Racer.
links.added: A Ferrari convertible, forking routes through varied scenery, and a choice of radio songs.
links.extra: Suzuki scouted Europe for two weeks in a BMW for ideas.

links.took: Pole Position popularized the behind-the-car racing view and checkpoint time limits.
links.added: A road trip instead of a circuit, with forks in the road choosing the next stage.
links.extra: IGN credits Pole Position with introducing checkpoints.

links.took: Out Run's sports-car fantasy on open roads with traffic.
links.added: A cockpit view, gear changes and police radar on a winding mountain road.

src.t: Wikipedia: Out Run (cites Luke Reilly, IGN)

links.extra: IGN's Luke Reilly lists Test Drive among games that contain elements of Out Run.

links.took: Exotic cars racing along scenic roads through traffic.
links.added: Real cars tuned with Road & Track magazine, police chases and 3D tracks.

src.t: Wikipedia: Out Run (cites Luke Reilly, IGN)

links.took: The pleasure of stylish cars on scenic real-world roads.
links.added: Kudos points for driving with style through recreated city streets.

src.t: Wikipedia: Out Run (cites Luke Reilly, IGN)

links.took: Arcade speed through busy traffic on public roads.
links.added: Slow-motion crashes and a boost meter filled by risky driving.

src.t: Wikipedia: Out Run (cites Luke Reilly, IGN)

links.took: The joy of a scenic drive with music playing.
links.added: An open-world festival in Colorado with radio stations and hundreds of licensed cars.

src.t: Wikipedia: Out Run (cites Luke Reilly, IGN)

links.took: Choosing which music to listen to on the car radio.
links.added: Full radio stations with DJs and adverts, inside a crime game's open city.

src.t: Wikipedia: Out Run (cites Jacopo Prisco, Wired UK)

links.extra: Wired UK points to Out Run's song choice as a forerunner of the car radio in Grand Theft Auto.

links.took: Out Run popularized into-the-screen road racing with hills, curves and roadside scenery.
links.added: Split-screen two-player races and a licensed Lotus Esprit on home computers.

links.took: Out Run popularized into-the-screen road racing over hills past roadside scenery.
links.added: A permanent split screen, fuel and pit stops, and a race tour across many countries.

links.took: The look of 16-bit road racers; Top Gear composer Barry Leitch scored the game.
links.added: Low-poly 3D tracks on a world tour, made for phones.
links.extra: Leitch was approached because Top Gear's soundtrack was popular with Brazilian players.

links.took: Out Run's sunny arcade road racing over hills.
links.added: Low-poly 3D graphics and a long world tour designed for touchscreens.
links.extra: Wikipedia describes it as inspired by 16-bit games like Top Gear and Out Run.

links.took: Behind-the-bike motorcycle racing; designer Dan Geisler felt Hang-On was 'limited' and wanted to surpass it.
links.added: Fistfights and clubs between riders, police, and long races on public roads.

src.t: Wikipedia: Road Rash (1991), citing Dan Geisler

links.extra: Geisler said Road Rash would make Hang-On 'obsolete'.

links.took: Motorbike racing where riders fight each other with weapons at speed.
links.added: A roguelike campaign with upgrades between races, and guns alongside melee weapons.

src.t: Wikipedia: Road Redemption (cites Eurogamer and PC Gamer)

links.extra: Described as a spiritual successor to Road Rash.

links.took: Road Rash's engine and its mix of racing and combat.
links.added: Inline skates instead of motorbikes, hitching rides on passing cars for speed.

links.took: Namco's own racing line: Ridge Racer began as an F1 game like Pole Position and Final Lap.
links.added: Texture-mapped 3D mountain roads, drifting, and one course with several variations.

links.took: Polygon 3D driving on a stunt course with a loop and jumps.
links.added: A track and terrain editor so players could build their own stunt courses.
links.extra: Wikipedia says Stunts was influenced by the arcade game Hard Drivin'.

links.took: Distinctive Software's earlier sports-car driving and cockpit view.
links.added: Polygon 3D tracks with loops, plus a full track editor.

links.took: Its gameplay, from shared developers: exotic cars on public roads with traffic and police.
links.added: 3D tracks, handling matched with Road & Track magazine, and authentic gear-change sounds.
links.extra: Wikipedia: 'Inspiration for the gameplay came from Test Drive, which had shared development staff.'

links.took: Hard Drivin' helped popularize filled-polygon 3D driving in arcades.
links.added: Fast polygon racing on Sega's Model 1 board, with four switchable camera views.
links.extra: Wikipedia notes Winning Run and Hard Drivin' came first, without claiming direct influence.

links.took: Sega AM2's Virtua Racing experience with lighting and switchable camera views.
links.added: Texture-mapped graphics on the new Model 2 board, NASCAR-style ovals and linked cabinets.

links.took: A rival to beat: Sega mandated that Daytona USA be better than Ridge Racer.
links.added: 'Funky' arcade entertainment in place of Ridge Racer's simulation style, with stock cars.

links.took: The same core team and parts of Motor Toon's engine, including its physics model.
links.added: Real licensed cars, licence tests and tuning, after five years of work under Kazunori Yamauchi.

links.took: The realistic car-collecting sim it set out to beat: 'we are targeting Gran Turismo'.
links.added: Online racing on Xbox Live, visible damage and a 'Drivatar' AI that learns your driving.

src.t: Kiki Wolfkill (Microsoft), quoted in Wikipedia: Forza Motorsport (2005)

links.extra: Wolfkill added: 'We have a lot of respect for Gran Turismo, which helps drive that desire to beat them.'

links.took: A collect-and-upgrade loop; the team 'played a lot of Diablo II' while planning a car-collecting game.
links.added: Cars instead of loot: earn credits, then buy, tune and paint real cars.

src.t: Dan Greenawalt (Turn 10), quoted in Wikipedia: Forza Motorsport (2005)

links.extra: Greenawalt said the team 'played a lot of Animal Crossing and Diablo II' while aiming for a 'car collecting game'.

links.took: Collecting as a reason to keep coming back; the team 'played a lot of Animal Crossing'.
links.added: A garage of real cars to collect, paint and tune.

src.t: Dan Greenawalt (Turn 10), quoted in Wikipedia: Forza Motorsport (2005)

links.extra: Greenawalt named both games while describing his aim of a 'car collecting game'.

links.took: Gran Turismo's licence tests, tuning and huge list of real cars.
links.added: More than 700 cars, the Nürburgring Nordschleife and a photo mode.

links.took: Gran Turismo's simulation racing, car collecting and licence tests.
links.added: A café whose menu books teach car history, and a full single-player career again after GT Sport.
links.extra: Gran Turismo 5, 6 and Sport came in between.

links.took: Forza's licensed cars, handling and tuning, built in collaboration with Turn 10.
links.added: An open world in Colorado, a music festival setting and street races between events.

links.took: The Horizon festival format: open-world driving, radio stations and hundreds of cars.
links.added: Britain as the map, with seasons that change the world every week.
links.extra: Forza Horizon 2 and 3 came in between.

links.took: Bizarre Creations' Kudos system for stylish driving, and recreated city streets.
links.added: Xbox power for New York, plus London, Tokyo and San Francisco, and more cars.

links.took: Its car handling: producer Guy Wilday said the game's basic premise 'was based around' Sega Rally.
links.added: Real World Rally Championship cars and drivers, and long point-to-point stages.

src.t: Wikipedia: Sega Rally Championship (cites Guy Wilday, Codemasters)

links.extra: Codemasters cited Sega Rally Championship as a strong influence.

links.took: Codemasters' rally simulation and stage-by-stage championships.
links.added: Rallycross, hill climbs and off-road trucks alongside traditional rally stages.
links.extra: Several Colin McRae Rally sequels came in between.

links.took: Criterion's high-speed traffic racing, with boost earned by risky driving.
links.added: Takedowns: ramming rivals off the road to earn boost, plus a crash mode.
links.extra: Burnout 2: Point of Impact (2002) came in between.

links.took: Criterion's crash-heavy arcade driving and its online-connected design.
links.added: Police chases with both cop and racer careers, and Autolog friend rivalries.

links.took: The Hot Pursuit idea: exotic cars racing while police try to stop them.
links.added: Gadgets like spike strips and EMPs for both racers and police in fictional Seacrest County.
links.extra: A reboot of the 1998 game's premise by a different studio.

updates.why: The Need for Speed first came out on the 3DO in December 1994; PC and console ports followed in 1995-96 (Wikipedia: The Need for Speed).
Tekken 3 launched in Japanese arcades in March 1997; the PlayStation version followed in 1998.
Street Fighter IV launched in Japanese arcades in July 2008; console versions followed in February 2009.
Created by Dino Dini, whom Wikipedia lists as developer; Anco published it.
